title: Low mood review with suicidal thoughts

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hi Daniel, come in. Thanks for coming back. And who's this with you?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is my sister, Laura. I asked her to come.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Hi.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hi Laura, thanks for coming. Daniel, is it okay for Laura to stay for the whole appointment?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yeah, that's fine. I want her here.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay. So last time we met, about four weeks ago, we started sertraline. How have things been since then?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Honestly, not great. Maybe a tiny bit better in the mornings, but mostly the same.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How long would you say you've been feeling low now, in total?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Since the summer. About three months.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And how is your mood on a scale of nought to ten, if ten is the best you've felt?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Three, maybe. Some days two.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How are you sleeping?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Badly. I wake at four and just lie there.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And your appetite?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Not really eating. I've lost about half a stone, I think.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Are you still off work?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yeah. I'm a warehouse supervisor, and I'm signed off for another two weeks.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'd like to ask about some difficult thoughts, if that's okay. When people feel this low, sometimes they have thoughts that life isn't worth living. Have you had thoughts like that?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yeah. Most days, the last couple of weeks. I think it'd be easier if I just didn't wake up.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thank you for telling me that. Have you had any thoughts of ending your life, or of harming yourself?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Not like actually doing anything. I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Have you made any plans, or done anything to prepare, like getting hold of tablets?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No. Nothing like that.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What stops you, would you say?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My nephew, Laura's boy. And my mum. I couldn't do that to them.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: He's really close to Alfie.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: That's really important. Have you ever harmed yourself or tried to end your life in the past?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, never.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Can I ask about alcohol? How much are you drinking at the moment?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe four pints a week.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Dan. It's four a night. I've seen the cans.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yeah. All right. Most nights, four cans. Sometimes more at the weekend.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thank you for being honest, both of you. Alcohol can really pull mood down and make thoughts like these feel stronger, so it's something I'd like us to work on.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I know.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any drugs, cannabis or anything else?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Have you had any side effects from the sertraline?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A bit of nausea the first week, that's gone now.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any feeling more agitated or restless since starting it?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, not really.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And you're taking it every day? Fifty milligrams in the morning?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Every morning, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any other medicines, and any allergies?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, and no allergies.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay. Looking at you today, Daniel, you look tired, your eye contact is reduced and your speech is a bit slow, but you're talking clearly and making sense. There's no sign of anything like hearing voices. Your PHQ-9 score today is 19.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is that bad?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: It tells me the depression is still moderately severe. After four weeks with only a small improvement, I think we should increase the sertraline to 100 milligrams once a day.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'd also like to refer you to the talking therapies service, and I'll give you the details to self-refer today as well. And I'd like to get the community mental health crisis team to know about you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Do I have to?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I think it's the safest thing for now, given the thoughts you've been having. I'd also like to see you again in one week, not four.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Let's agree a plan for if things get worse. If the thoughts get stronger, or you start thinking about acting on them, call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or the Samaritans on 116 123, any time of day. If you feel you can't keep yourself safe, call 999 or go to A&E.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I'll put those in my phone too.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: That's great, Laura. Would you be willing to keep any stockpiled medicines out of the house, or have Laura look after them?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yeah, that's fine.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And let's try to cut down the alcohol gradually. I'll give you the details for the local alcohol support service.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. Thanks.

reference_note.presenting_complaint: Review of low mood, 4 weeks after starting sertraline.
reference_note.history: Low mood for about 3 months. Slight improvement in mornings only; mood 2–3/10. Early morning waking at 4 am. Reduced appetite with approximately half a stone weight loss. Works as a warehouse supervisor; currently signed off for a further two weeks. Reports passive suicidal ideation (would be easier not to wake up) most days for the last two weeks. No active suicidal thoughts, plans or preparations. No previous self-harm or suicide attempts. Protective factors: nephew and mother. Alcohol: initially said four pints a week; on sister's challenge, confirmed four cans most nights, more at weekends. No drug use. Mild nausea in first week of sertraline, now resolved; no agitation. Attended with sister, with consent.
reference_note.medications_allergies: Sertraline 50 mg once daily (4 weeks). No known drug allergies.
reference_note.examination: Appears tired, reduced eye contact, slowed speech. Speech coherent. No psychotic features. PHQ-9: 19.
reference_note.impression: Moderately severe depression with partial response to sertraline. Passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent; protective factors present. Harmful alcohol use.
reference_note.plan: Increase sertraline to 100 mg once daily. Refer to NHS Talking Therapies and self-referral details given. Inform the community crisis team. Review in 1 week. Agreed to hand stockpiled medicines to sister. Alcohol support service details given; aim to reduce gradually.
reference_note.safety_netting: Crisis plan agreed: if thoughts worsen or he considers acting on them, call NHS 111 (mental health option) or Samaritans 116 123; if unable to keep himself safe, call 999 or attend A&E. Sister has the numbers.
